prompt: What is the name of the one-minute formative-assessment technique, from Angelo and Cross's 'Classroom Assessment Techniques,' that asks a learner to write down the single thing that is still least clear at the end of a lesson?

Have a peer or mentor evaluate your workshop/lesson design from this lesson's step 2 against this rubric: (1) the learning objectives are checkable actions ('learner can explain/write/predict X'), not vague states like 'understand X'; (2) you name a specific, real misconception (from Qian & Lehman's literature review, or your own direct observation) that the lesson design preempts, and say exactly how; (3) the demo or hook makes the concept observable rather than just asserted. Paste your worksheet and have them mark each of the three criteria pass/fail with one sentence of reasoning each.

Write a 200-300 word account of your closed feedback loop from step 6: the muddiest-point confusion signal you got from a real beginner, the recurring misconception pattern from your Exercism mentoring discussions, the single concrete change you made to your material because of both, and what happened when a second real beginner went through the revised version. Have a peer or mentor critique it against this rubric: does it name a specific change (not 'I clarified things'), does it connect the change to actual evidence rather than a hunch, and does it honestly report whether the revision helped, including if it didn't fully work?

Have an Exercism mentoring lead, a peer mentor, or a study partner read three of your real mentor discussion threads from step 5 and evaluate them against this rubric: in each thread, did you ask a question that could lead the student to their own fix before offering one directly; does at least one comment across the three address a conceptual misunderstanding rather than a style or syntax nit; and could a reader who wasn't there tell, from the thread text alone, what the student actually learned by the end of it?
